content: 1. Intramuscular (IM) refers to a method of administering medication directly into the muscle tissue. 2. Subcutaneous (SC) refers to a method of administering medication beneath the skin, into the fatty tissue. 3. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is a type of scientific study that randomly assigns participants to different groups to compare the effects of interventions. 4. Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use are guidelines that determine the safety and appropriateness of contraceptive methods for individuals with specific medical conditions. 5. A study by Kaunitz et al. compared the contraceptive efficacy and effects on bone mineral density of subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA-SC) versus intramuscular DMPA (DMPA-IM) over two years. 6. Arias et al. investigated changes in bleeding patterns associated with the use of 104 mg subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injections. 7. Westhoff et al. examined the pharmacokinetics and ovulation suppression effects of a lower-dose subcutaneous formulation of Depo-Provera. 8. Crosignani et al. compared the effectiveness of subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate and leuprolide acetate in managing endometriosis-associated pain. 9. Schlaf et al. conducted a study comparing subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate with leuprolide acetate for treating endometriosis-related pain. 10. Polis et al. evaluated the preference for Sayana® Press (a subcutaneous contraceptive) versus intramuscular Depo-Provera among HIV-positive women in Uganda through a randomized crossover trial. 11. Jain et al. assessed the contraceptive efficacy and safety of DMPA-SC in a study published in 2004. 12. Segall-Gutierrez et al. studied the effects of subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate on follicular development and ovulation in extremely obese women. 13. Another study by Segall-Gutierrez et al. examined the impact of DMPA-SC on serum androgen markers in women of varying body weights. 14. Segall-Gutierrez et al. also investigated the deterioration of cardiometabolic risk markers in obese women using depot medroxyprogesterone acetate. 15. A pilot study by Segall-Gutierrez et al. explored short-term changes in bone mineral density among class 3 obese users of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate. 16. Goldstein et al. conducted a pilot study on the effects of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate on coagulation parameters. 17. Recommendations for the safety of Sino-implant (II) for women with medical conditions align with the World Health Organization’s eligibility criteria for contraceptive use. 18. Studies comparing Sino-implant (II) with other levonorgestrel implants found no significant differences in safety profiles or serious adverse events. 19. Evidence suggests that Sino-implant (II) is not harmful and may be beneficial for women with menorrhagia. 20. The Sino-implant (II) does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV, and consistent condom use is recommended for STI prevention. 21. Women have the right to access evidence-based, comprehensive contraceptive information to make informed choices about their reproductive health. 22. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) are not applicable for pregnant women, but accidental use does not harm the woman, pregnancy, or fetus. 23. Breastfeeding women can use combined oral contraceptives (COCs) or levonorgestrel (LNG) regimens for ECPs without restriction. However, breastfeeding is not recommended for one week after taking ulipristal acetate (UPA) due to its excretion in breast milk. Breast milk should be expressed and discarded during this period.
